result:
Solution 2 is correct. Its upper bound and its construction both hold up.

**Setup.** A $k$-vertex induced subgraph $F$ contains $K_{1,k-1}$ exactly when it has a vertex of degree $k-1$. It is contained in $K_{1,k-1}$ exactly when all its edges share one vertex. So in an exact graph $G$, every $k$-set must induce either the star itself or a graph with $\Delta\le k-2$ whose edges do not all share a vertex.

**Upper bound.**
- No independent $k$-set exists, since the empty graph is contained in the star. So $\alpha(G)\le k-1$.
- If $\alpha(G)=k-1$, take an independent set $I$ of size $k-1$. Any vertex $v\notin I$ must be adjacent to all of $I$. Otherwise $I\cup\{v\}$ induces a star plus isolated vertices, which is forbidden. Such a $v$ has degree at least $k-1$, so $N(v)$ must be independent (otherwise $v$, an edge in $N(v)$, and further neighbours induce a proper supergraph of the star). If two vertices outside $I$ were adjacent, one would lie in the other's neighbourhood together with $I$, and it is adjacent to $I$, contradicting independence. So $V\setminus I$ is independent, and $n\le 2k-2\le (k-1)(k-2)$ for $k\ge 4$.
- If $\alpha(G)\le k-2$, a vertex of degree at least $k-1$ would have an independent neighbourhood of size at least $k-1>\alpha$, which is impossible. So $\Delta\le k-2$, and $n\le(\Delta+1)\alpha\le(k-1)(k-2)$.

**Construction.** Take $(k-2)K_{k-1}$, which has $(k-1)(k-2)$ vertices. A $k$-subset induces at most $k-2$ nonempty cliques with sizes summing to $k$.
- If some clique has at least 3 vertices, the induced graph contains a triangle, so it is not a subgraph of the star. Since $\Delta\le k-2$, it does not contain the star either, so it is incomparable.
- Otherwise all cliques have size at most 2, which gives at least $k-(k-2)=2$ disjoint edges. Again neither containment holds.

So $f(K_{1,k-1})=(k-1)(k-2)$.

Solution 1 is wrong because $K_{k-1,k-1}$ gives only $2k-2$, which is not the maximum. Solution 3 gives $k^2-k+1$, which exceeds the proven upper bound.

CHOICE: 2
